source.title: Identifying Mislabeled Data using the Area Under the Margin Ranking
source.authors: Geoff Pleiss; Tianyi Zhang; Ethan R. Elenberg; Kilian Q. Weinberger

record.file_problem: Full paper and supplementary information provided; text is readable.
record.tranche_reason: Tests how removing examples ranked as mislabeled by training dynamics changes test error on synthetic noisy and real-world image datasets; this is a new setting relative to the mapped versions.
record.gate_note: The study reports results for removing AUM-identified training examples and for AUM ranking consistency across architectures. It does not test the listed memorization/generalization conditions directly. Baseline and comparison-method results are included only where they compare the outcome of the AUM removal intervention. Cited findings are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study uses random-label memorization as motivation for identifying mislabeled examples and evaluates its AUM cleaning method. It tests none of V1–V8. In particular, low AUM is not V8's inclusion-based memorization score, and removing low-AUM examples does not test removal of the most memorized examples.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors conclude that AUM and artificial threshold samples identify mislabeled or harmful data and that cleaning improves performance on many noisy and relatively clean datasets. They report architecture and threshold robustness, limited recall under strong asymmetric noise, and no significant ImageNet improvement.
record.recipe_differences: The study changes the training data by adding artificial threshold samples to measure AUM, then removes low-AUM examples and retrains. It does not reproduce the listed interventions or measurements in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with dataset, synthetic noise rate, and noise structure. The authors report lower recall at 30% and 40% asymmetric noise; AUM removal did not significantly change ImageNet top-1 error. With 40% CIFAR10 noise, removal reduces error under both augmentation and no augmentation. Threshold percentile changes outcomes, with higher percentiles typically better on 40% noisy CIFAR100.

fits_no_version.finding: Removing low-AUM examples lowers test error across the recorded uniformly noisy datasets and several real-world datasets. ImageNet shows no significant change.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: AUM-based dataset cleaning can improve image-classification accuracy, with benefits depending on the dataset and noise structure.

fits_no_version.finding: On unmodified and 40%-noisy CIFAR100, AUM-ranked removal has an optimum near the proposed threshold; random removal increases error.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The effect of removing training examples depends on their AUM ranking and the removal threshold.

fits_no_version.finding: AUM rankings correlate approximately 0.97–0.98 across the tested ResNet and DenseNet architectures.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: AUM training-example rankings are consistent across the tested convolutional architectures.

record.problems: The authors state that AUM struggles with highly systematic asymmetric noise, with recall struggling at 30% and 40% noise and performance not competitive with the best method at 40%. Larger datasets have only a single trial; test-error on ImageNet does not significantly change. The figure-only CIFAR100 removal sweep provides no exact values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported rows omitted; the AUM ranking sweep in Figure 5 is retained as one textual aggregate row because exact plotted values are not available in the supplied text. The paper also reports baselines and competing methods, but those methods are not the study's AUM removal intervention.

untested.parts: No paired demonstration of random-label fitting, natural-label generalization, and chance held-out performance with random labels.
No width sweep beyond the width needed for zero training error; double descent is proposed as future work.
No convolutional versus fully connected generalization comparison or local-connectivity intervention.
No adaptive optimizer versus SGD comparison.
Batch size changes accompany AUM measurement and dataset cleaning, but no controlled batch-size generalization comparison is reported.
No dropout intervention or joint dropout and weight-decay removal.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measurement or comparison of its ability to rank generalization gaps.
No inclusion-based memorization estimation or removal of the highest-memorization examples versus matched random removal.

record.verdict_notes: States are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8 because every row measures a different construct or intervention. These method-performance rows do not warrant claim-version verdicts. The text also reports full Clothing1M and asymmetric-noise cleaning results absent from the record, but neither bears on a listed version.

versions.untested_parts: Does not compare fitting random labels with generalization on natural labels.
No width sweep beyond interpolation or test-error measurement across widths.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
No large-batch versus small-batch generalization comparison.
AUM is a training-sample margin ranking; the study does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or compare generalization-gap predictors.
Does not remove examples according to how much their inclusion raises the chance of predicting their own labels.
